Keywords: Was, Who, Tho

outputs.L1:
A physician of eminence, some years ago,  
Was summoned to attend a lady of fashion,  
Long admired, and once the toast of every beau,  
Though now her sunken features stirred compassion.  

No sooner had the doctor observed the lady’s face  
Than he begged that, for once, she would pardon his candour,  
If he departed from the rules of polite decorum  
To state the terms on which her life might endure.  

“By all means,” cried the lady, “for surely no word  
A physician may utter should ever give offence;  
Punctilio in illness is always absurd,  
And proves that either doctor or patient lacks sense.”  

“Then, my dear lady, I cannot resist  
Declaring this truth, as a plain, honest man:  
If you persist in the use of white paint,  
No medicine will save you, despite all I can do.”  

“You astonish me, Doctor! Yet such is my case  
That I may as well die as give up painting;  
For should I appear with my natural face  
Among my acquaintances, I should not be known.”
outputs.L2:
Some years back, a highly respected doctor was summoned to treat a fashionable lady. She had long been celebrated and praised by every admirer, though her now-collapsed features made people pity her instead.

As soon as the physician had examined her, he asked her to excuse him if, just this once, he set aside the usual rules of politeness and spoke plainly about what she must do if she wished to survive.

“Certainly,” the lady replied. “Nothing a doctor says ought to be taken as an insult. Formal ceremony during sickness is ridiculous, and only proves that either the doctor or the patient lacks good sense.”

“In that case, madam,” said the doctor, “I must honestly tell you the truth: if you continue using white face paint, no treatment I can give you will preserve your life.”

“You amaze me, Doctor,” she answered. “But my situation is such that I might just as well die as give up painting my face. If I were to appear among my acquaintances with my natural complexion, no one would recognize me.”
outputs.L3:
A respected physician was once called to attend a fashionable lady whose beauty had long been admired in society. In former years, her appearance had been praised wherever she went, but now that beauty had faded under the effects of illness. Her friends were alarmed by her condition, and the physician was summoned in the hope that his skill might restore her health.

After examining her carefully, the doctor saw that her illness was serious. Before offering his advice, however, he asked her permission to speak with complete frankness. He explained that, if she truly wished to recover, she must be willing to hear the truth about the habits that were harming her. Without such honesty, he could give her no useful treatment.

The lady replied that a physician’s sincerity ought never to give offense, especially when a patient’s life was at stake. She assured him that he might speak freely, since illness was not a time for flattery or concealment.

Thus encouraged, the doctor told her plainly that no medicine would save her unless she abandoned the use of white face paint. He warned her that the cosmetics she applied so constantly were damaging her health and worsening her condition. If she continued to cover her face in this way, all his prescriptions would be useless.

The lady listened to his warning, but instead of accepting it, she answered with pride and distress. She said that she would rather die than appear in her natural complexion. Without the paint, she declared, her acquaintances would not even recognize her. To her, losing the artificial appearance by which society knew her seemed worse than losing her life.
outputs.L4:
A fashionable lady, once admired in every drawing room for the brilliance of her complexion and the elegance of her appearance, fell dangerously ill. Her friends were alarmed, for the sickness did not pass quickly, and her strength declined from day to day. At last, a physician of great reputation was called to attend her.

After examining her carefully, he prescribed medicines and instructed her to follow a strict regimen. But before leaving, he noticed the thick layer of white paint on her face—the very cosmetic she had long used to preserve the appearance of youth and beauty.

“Madam,” he said plainly, “if you wish to recover, you must give up this face paint at once. It is harming you. So long as you continue to cover your skin with it, all my remedies will be useless.”

The lady listened with visible distress, not because of the danger to her life, but because of what his advice would require of her. To appear before others with her natural complexion seemed to her a humiliation worse than sickness itself.

After a moment, she replied, “Then let me die. I would rather go to my grave painted than live and show the world my real face.”

The physician could say no more. Her answer revealed that her illness was not only of the body, but also of the mind and spirit. She had become so enslaved by fashion, vanity, and the expectations of society that life itself seemed less valuable than the false appearance she had struggled to maintain.

Thus the story shows how destructive vanity can become when a person values admiration more than health, truth, or life. Beauty that depends on deceit may win applause for a time, but it can also demand a terrible price from those who cannot bear to live without it.
outputs.L5:
**Was, Who, Tho**

There was a moment when everything felt uncertain. The past was full of questions, the present was moving too fast, and the future seemed impossible to predict. People kept asking, “Who are you becoming?” but the answer was not always clear.

Who we are is often shaped by what we have been through. Every mistake, every lesson, and every quiet victory becomes part of the story. Sometimes we look back and wonder who we were before life changed us.

Tho, even when the path feels confusing, there is still meaning in the journey. Growth does not always happen loudly. Sometimes it happens in small choices, in silent courage, and in the decision to keep going.

What was behind us matters, but it does not define everything. Who we choose to become matters even more. And tho the road may not always be easy, it can still lead somewhere beautiful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an 18th-century style satirical poem about a fashionable lady whose doctor warns her that her use of white face paint is killing her, but she refuses to stop because no one would recognize her natural face.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Lady’s Last Complexion**

Behold Clarinda, Toast of Mall and Play,  
Whose face outshone the artificial day;  
So bright with white, so delicately dead,  
One scarce could tell her cheek from powdered lead.  

Her doctor came, with solemn wig and cane,  
And felt her pulse, and shook his head in pain:  
“Madam,” quoth he, “this bloom you daily spread  
Steals from your breath and lodges in your head.  

This snowy paste, which makes the beaux adore,  
Will close your eyes and rouge your lips no more;  
Your glass may flatter, and your fans may lie,  
But paint so fair persuades the fair to die.”  

Clarinda sighed, then touched a patch awry,  
And raised to Heaven one well-enamelled eye:  
“Good Doctor, preach of death to those who choose;  
I cannot live if I my face should lose.  

Were I to wash, and Nature stand confess’d,  
My footman’s self would know me not undress’d;  
My friends would start, my lovers flee the place,  
And ask what stranger stole Clarinda’s face.  

No, let the grave receive me smooth and white,  
A finished beauty, fit for candlelight;  
Since all the world my borrowed charms approve,  
I’ll die well-painted, though I cannot move.”  

Thus Fashion reigns, where Reason pleads in vain,  
And health is sold for one admiring swain;  
The belle, who feared no coffin, shroud, nor bier,  
Could only dread her own complexion clear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed comic verse in the manner of an old moral anecdote, featuring a physician, a vain society woman, and a punchline about cosmetics.
counterfactuals.output:
A doctor, grave, with silver cane,  
Was called through sleet and sooty rain  
To view a dame of high degree,  
As vain as any dame could be.  

She sighed, “Good sir, I fade, I fear;  
My cheek grows pale, my eye less clear.  
Prescribe me youth—be quick, be kind—  
And leave no wrinkle-line behind!”  

He felt her pulse, surveyed her face,  
Her ribbons, rouge, and costly lace,  
Then said, “Madam, the case is plain:  
You court too much, and sleep too vain.  

Rise with the lark, shun midnight routs,  
Take simple meals and country bouts;  
Let honest air your bloom renew,  
And bid your looking-glass adieu.”  

She cried, “How coarse! How very odd!  
Must beauty walk upon the sod?  
No, doctor—name a finer art:  
Some secret draught to mend the heart!”  

He bowed, and wrote, with solemn care,  
A physic rare beyond compare:  
“Apply each morn, for all your flaws,  
Less paint upon the face—more pause.”  

She read, and frowned, “This cure I doubt!”  
“Then, madam,” said he, turning out,  
“Since Nature’s claim you still dispute,  
Try cosmetics—for the soul, not suit.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Georgian-era poetic fable about a lady of fashion being told by her doctor that her makeup is dangerous, ending with her saying she would rather die than be seen without it.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Lady and the Doctor**

In days when hoops like planets swung,  
And patches spoke what lips had sung,  
A Lady, bright as noon in May,  
Rouged dawn and candled night away.  

Her cheeks outblushed the damask rose,  
Her brows were black as chimney-crows;  
With pearl and powder, paste and paint,  
She looked half Venus, half a saint.  

But soon a Doctor, grave and thin,  
With cane in hand and solemn chin,  
Observed her bloom, too fiercely red,  
And shook his peruke-fragrant head.  

“Madam,” quoth he, “these arts you use  
Will steal the life they seem to choose.  
That charming white, that scarlet dye,  
Are poisons laid to please the eye.  

Your leaden wash, your cordial glow,  
May bring you beauty—and bring you low;  
Take Nature’s hue, dismiss the jar,  
Be less an angel, live the more.”  

The Lady laughed behind her fan:  
“Good sir, prescribe to whom you can.  
Shall I, who rule the Mall and ball,  
Appear with no complexion at all?  

Let shepherdesses plainness prize,  
Let dairymaids have honest eyes;  
A face unpainted may be pure—  
But who could possibly endure?  

No, Doctor, keep your draught and sigh;  
Your warnings cannot make me fly.  
Since Fashion is the breath I draw,  
I own her empire, crown, and law.  

If rouge must kill, then let it be;  
A ghastlier fate I plainly see:  
For, sir, I swear by powder, patch, and fan—  
I’d rather die than be seen without it by man.”  

**Moral:**  
When vanity is made a creed,  
Good counsel seldom finds its seed;  
And she who lives by Fashion’s breath  
May choose appearance—even to death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a four-stanza humorous poem with alternating rhymes about vanity, where a doctor advises a once-beautiful socialite to stop using white paint.
counterfactuals.output:
Madame Celeste, once the belle of the ball,  
Now powdered her face like a fence in the lane;  
She swept through the town with a ghostly white pall,  
And left little flakes on the window and train.  

Her doctor looked over his spectacles wide,  
And coughed as she shimmered in chalky delight;  
“Your pulse would improve,” he advised with some pride,  
“If you’d stop painting yourself quite so white.”  

“But Doctor,” she cried, “I was famed for my glow!  
The poets all praised me, the dukes were polite!”  
He said, “Yes, but now, when the north breezes blow,  
The pigeons line up for a perch overnight.”  

So Madame went home and abandoned the brush,  
Her mirror complained, but her cheeks turned all right;  
And though she still entered each room with a hush,  
At least no one mistook her for walls in the night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**The Lady’s Physick**

“Madam,” quoth leech, with solemn brow,  
“Thy case is plain, I tell thee now:  
These washes, ceruse, rouge, and dye,  
Do paint thee fair, but bid thee die.

Thy cheek, so bravely damask’d o’er,  
Is but a sign above Death’s door;  
This pearl, this bloom, this borrow’d grace,  
Are grave-cloths fitted to thy face.

Cast off these poisons, patch, and paint;  
Be wan, be wrinkled, be a saint;  
For if thou still with art contend,  
Thy beauty brings thee to thine end.”

She heard, and shook her powder’d head,  
Then simper’d sweet, and sighing said:  
“Good Doctor, let the sexton come—  
I’ll rather perish thus than hum.

For should I wash these charms away,  
And meet my friends at noon of day,  
So strange a face would greet their view,  
They’d cry, ‘Pray, Madam, who are you?’”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
